questions.q: According to the lesson, why is it necessary to clamp pixel values to the range [0, 1] after operations like normalization?
options: To ensure the values are integers for storage
Because light cannot be negative or exceed 100% white in standard 8-bit space
To increase the resolution of the image
To convert the tensor from float32 to uint8
questions.answer: Because light cannot be negative or exceed 100% white in standard 8-bit space
questions.why: The lesson states: 'Light cannot be negative. Light cannot be "more than 100% white" in standard 8-bit space. We must force these values back into the [0, 1] box.'

questions.q: In the context of PyTorch convolutions described in the lesson, what is the preferred tensor shape order for images?
questions.why: The lesson explicitly states: 'PyTorch convolutions prefer [B, C, H, W].'

questions.q: What is the mathematical formula provided in the lesson for scaling an integer pixel value $x$ (in range 0-255) to a float value $y$ (in range 0-1)?
questions.why: The 'Under the hood' section defines the scaling mechanism with the formula: $y = \frac{x}{255.0}$.

questions.q: According to the 'Common mistakes' section, what visual artifact occurs if you permute an image to [B, W, H, C] instead of [B, H, W, C] for a rectangular image?
options: The image will be transposed or rotated 90 degrees
The image loses its color channels
questions.answer: The image will be transposed or rotated 90 degrees
questions.why: The lesson states: 'If you permute to [B, W, H, C] instead of [B, H, W, C], your image will be transposed... a rectangular one will be rotated 90 degrees.'

questions.q: Why does the lesson advise converting `uint8` to `float32` once at the start and keeping it as float until the very end?
options: Because converting back and forth loses precision
Because `float32` is required for all PyTorch operations
questions.answer: Because converting back and forth loses precision
questions.why: The lesson states: 'Converting back and forth loses precision. Do it once, at the start, and keep it as float until the very end.'
